Battlefield 6 kicks off its first free trial post the Black Ops 7 launch to twist that knife

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (388 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Vg247

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if you don’t care about the rivalries between the top multiplayer first-person shooters series, it’s hard to ignore how much EA wanted to stick it to Call of Duty this year with Battlefield 6.
  • Activision saw that coming early enough that it ran multiple free weekends around major moments for EA’s game, including its launch, seemingly in an effort to capture some of those players and keep them away from BF6.
  • Both Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 have now rolled out, and though exact sales figures may never be detrmined (though EA did announce 7 million sold in the first week), it’s very clear at this point from every metric we can see that BF6 came out on top this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you don’t care about the rivalries between the top multiplayer first-person shooters series, it’s hard to ignore how much EA wanted to stick it to Call of Duty this year with Battlefield 6.

Activision saw that coming early enough that it ran multiple free weekends around major moments for EA’s game, including its launch, seemingly in an effort to capture some of those players and keep them away from BF6.

Both Battlefield 6, and Black Ops 7 have now rolled out, and though exact sales figures may never be detrmined (though EA did announce 7 million sold in the first week), it’s very clear at this point from every metric we can see that BF6 came out on top this year.

The recent Black Ops 7 launch clearly hasn’t made many people happy, so just like Activision made Black Ops 6 free to play at BF6’s launch, EA has now done the same with its own game. The Battlefield 6 free trial, which was unveiled last week, is just an hour away at the time of this writing.

This is the first trial for the core game, and it arrives some six weeks after Battlefield 6 officialy rolled out, and four weeks following the release of the free-to-play Battlefield Redsec, which has battle royale and other components.

Beyond all the drama surrounding the two rival shooter franchises, the Battlefield 6 trial is itself pretty straightfoward, and is notably nowhere near as genrous as some of the Call of Duty ones we’ve seen recently.

Industry observers note that the trial goes live today at 4am PT, 7am ET, 12pm GMT across all platforms, and will be available for a week; ending Tuesday, December 2. It includes three core maps: Siege of Cairo, Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields.

Players will have access to four game modes, played on different versions of the same maps. Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch will all be available to choose from, and there don’t appear to be any level or XP limits in the trial.

Unfortunatley, just as the free trial was about to go live, the game got hit with a major matchmaking outage that took down all matchmaking in the core game, leaving Redsec unaffected.

Hopefully EA can resolve this problem before the trial officially kicks off.

Breaking: Aptera (SEV) completes its first customer solar EV — for its top crowdfunder

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (996 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer.
  • It’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022.
  • Aptera revealed today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that aptera (SEV) has finished building its first solar electric vehicle for a paying customer. It’s going to Martin Hartono, the startup’s No. 1 “Accelerator” investor, and it’s being exported out of the US.

It’s a real milestone for a company that has pushed back its delivery dates since 2022. And it comes a week after Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash against the roughly $25 million it says it needs to start series production.

Aptera revealed today from its Carlsbad, California headquarters that it completed what it calls its first production solar electric vehicle. The car is finished in “Noir,” a matte black exterior, and was built for Accelerator #1.

Recent findings suggest that accelerators are investors from Aptera’s community funding program, where delivery priority goes to whoever invests the most. So the first customer car went to the biggest check.

Hartono is the CEO of GDP Venture, the Jakarta-based venture arm of Indonesia’s Djarum Group. Aptera didn’t say which country the car is going to, what he paid for it, or when it will actually be handed over.

In the release, Hartono remarked Aptera is a fit for people who want to “minimize their energy consumption without compromising the ability to travel long distances.” Co-CEO Chris Anthony called it “the moment our team has worked toward for years” and said the company is working to finish more vehicles for early customers as soon as possible.

No number was given for how many more.

It has been revealed that the timing is interesting. Just seven weeks ago, Aptera cut its estimated cost to start production to about $25 million, down from $40 to $45 million, and noted the first 40 production vehicles would start building by the end of 2026, with customer deliveries in early 2027 “subject to financing.”.

Its Q3 report last week didn’t change that picture much. Aptera ended September with $9.2 million in cash, and $4.1 million of that is refundable reservation fees. It lost $14 million in the quarter, and its own filing indicates substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern “has not been alleviated.”.

In a recent development, on November 10, it priced a $6 million registered direct offering at $1.75 per share. SEV closed at $1.67 on Tuesday, with a 52-week high of $7.

The solar side of the pitch holds up better. In August, TÜV Rheinland measured 4.23 to 4.75 kWh per day going into the battery from the car’s integrated panels in Carlsbad, which works out to roughly 40 miles of daily driving. But that conversion relies on Aptera’s 100 Wh/mile efficiency target, and today’s release itself notes that figure isn’t yet confirmed for production vehicles.

The release’s risk factors are also worth reading. They list export, import, certification and registration requirements, state dealer licensing, single-source suppliers, and whether reservations will convert into binding orders. Shipping car No. 1 to an investor overseas sidesteps most of those for now.

Credit where it’s due. Aptera has a finished car built to a customer’s spec, which is more than Lightyear or Sono Motors ever got to before they ran out of money. We’ve followed this firm since it came back in 2019, and plenty of people (us included, at times) didn’t think we’d see this day.

A positive achievement, but the question remains: Is this essentially a hand-built prototype and a token delivery to one very rich customer, or is it the first of many more vehicles that will roll off an assembly line for regular people over the next couple months?

Industry observers note that but I have to be honest, this looks more symbolic than like the start of a production ramp. This is a single vehicle, built before Aptera has raised the money it claims it needs for series production, and it went to the person who put the most money into the company. That’s a thank-you and a good press release ahead of what will likely be another raise. It doesn’t tell us much about Aptera’s ability to build cars at a cost that works.

Industry observers note that the real test is still the first 40 cars, and whether they reach regular reservation holders in the US. Aptera claims it needs about $25 million to get there. It has $9.2 million, $4.1 million of which customers can ask back for, and it’s raising money at under $2 a share, which means a lot of dilution for every dollar.

According to recent reports, we want this to work. Ultra-efficient cars are the only way vehicle-integrated solar makes sense, and Aptera is the last serious attempt standing. So can it fund those 40 cars before the cash runs out?

Industry observers note that if you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, even if your car doesn’t have panels built into the body like the Aptera. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #109653. Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2461 w)

Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S.
  • So Shurcliff rolled out the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S.
  • In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

But no one else would. So Shurcliff rolled out the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The Newly introduced York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

It worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

In a recent development, today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if fresh engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

Sources indicate that during World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The Latest York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

When supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

The U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it said might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

Industry observers note that fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon launched its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

Recent findings suggest that sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

That restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

In a recent development, when a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

Sources indicate that in his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

Worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

In a recent development, on paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a big deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

If you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

Industry observers note that what no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

Recent findings suggest that in a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Recent findings suggest that despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters stated they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

Sources indicate that nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who said they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

In a recent development, although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff introduced the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The Latest York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

In a recent development, SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man new to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

Sources indicate that in 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

In 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars.

Robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

In 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

In 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

Concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

In July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a new supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

It has been revealed that private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

According to recent reports, the modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA intends to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

According to recent reports, since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

But Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

Even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a upcoming supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic says Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

In a recent development, shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The New York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

In A Century in Motion, Popular Science revisits fascinating transportation stories from our archives, from hybrid cars to moving sidewalks, and explores how these inventions are re-emerging today in surprising ways.

The 2027 Hyundai Elantra Is Bigger and Much, Much Bolder

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (624 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Hyundai Elantra continues to defy the apparent incipient death of the sedan, and the Korean automaker just gave it a major upgrade for 2027.
  • Revealed Thursday at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show, the 2027 Elantra's most obvious feature is its exterior design.
  • Industry observers note that “There is an inherent beauty in a sedan because its proportions are honest, intuitive and functional,” said SangYup Lee, executive vice president and head of the Hyundai and Genesis Global Design Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Hyundai Elantra continues to defy the apparent incipient death of the sedan, and the Korean automaker just gave it a major upgrade for 2027. Between a latest “Art of Steel” design, a larger size, and upgraded infotainment technology, the 2027 Hyundai Elantra is more prepared for the future than ever before.

Revealed Thursday at the 2026 Los Angeles Auto Show, the 2027 Elantra's most obvious feature is its exterior design. Created under Hyundai's newly introduced Art of Steel design philosophy, which was first revealed on the Boulder concept, the Elantra is now a boxy beast with wide fenders, sharp headlights, and a square rear end. This new sedan was designed with a very clear three-box configuration and sport sedan dynamism in mind, according to Hyundai’s head of design.

Industry observers note that “There is an inherent beauty in a sedan because its proportions are honest, intuitive and functional,” said SangYup Lee, executive vice president and head of the Hyundai and Genesis Global Design Center. “With the all-latest Elantra, we returned to that essence, then pushed it forward. Wide, muscular fenders, a long hood, and refined three-box proportions give Elantra a confident, athletic presence that challenges the conventions of the compact sedan.”.

In addition to the new exterior design, changes under the skin mean the latest Elantra is now 3.3 inches longer, 1.1 inches wider, and features a 1.1-inch longer wheelbase than its predecessor; all told, Hyundai indicates the 2027 Elantra has over one inch more rear headroom and legroom. So-called H-Edge lighting, futuristic grille styling, slim- neck mirrors, and lift-up flush door handles make up the rest of the visual changes.

But Hyundai didn’t stop its design renovations with the exterior. Inside the Elantra, the carmaker added a upcoming Curve of Upholstery design and an asymmetrical front layout, which is meant to “gently embrace” the driver. A central 12.9-inch Pleos Connect infotainment system is standard on all Elantra models, while an available slim information display in the driver’s natural line of sight provides critical driving information. Other interior features include 15-kW dual wireless phone charging, Audio by Bang & Olufsen, Hyundai Digital Key 2, and 100-watt ultra-fast charging USB ports. Upholstery will be available in four black color combinations, as well as Burgundy/Rose Ivory and Chalk Beige.

It has been revealed that mechanically, the Elantra is a bit less exciting. The newly introduced model will offer two powertrain options: a 1.6-liter hybrid four-cylinder powerplant, and a naturally-aspirated 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine. The hybrid model will deliver 154 horsepower through a six-speed dual-clutch transmission, while the purely internal combustion model offers 146 horsepower routed through a continuously variable transmission. Hybridized Elantra models also feature a predictive drive system that intelligently anticipates driving patterns and road conditions to maximize efficiency, as well as a new “Stay Mode” that lets the climate control, stereo, charging ports and other non-motion-related functions operate for up to 30 minutes with the engine off.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Machina’s business is based around its RoboCraftsman platform, which it basically pitches as a factory in a box.
  • Machina Labs was founded in 2019 and so far has mostly served clients in the aerospace and defense industries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that automotive manufacturing is a laborious, resource-intensive process. While the complex metropolises that are modern car factories work well for high-volume products, it is often prohibitively expensive for automakers to retool these plants to create distinct body panels for limited-production models. Now a California-based firm called Machina Labs aims to plug that gap with an innovative metal manufacturing process that promises speed, flexibility, and cost-savings.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

Machina’s business is based around its RoboCraftsman platform, which it basically pitches as a factory in a box. The system uses a pair of large robotic arms to perform a variety of tasks on metal panels, from striking designs into pre-stamped panels to fully forming new pieces. The robotic arms are controlled by software that can switch between different projects as swiftly as Machina can upload new designs, and the system also scans the completed panel to see if any additional work needs to be done, and to trim, finish, and heat treat the pieces. The entire setup can be folded into two shipping containers that can then be easily transported.

Machina Labs was founded in 2019 and so far has mostly served clients in the aerospace and defense industries. But now Machina wants to enter the automotive space, launching a new division called Machina Rebellis. With its RoboCraftsman platform, Machina aims to give automakers a way to skip the costly retooling process, with its technology providing a more efficient method to promptly craft customizable body panels, allowing OEMs to efficiently build more distinctive limited-edition cars.

Machina’s interest in the automotive world started a few years back when it built a truck called the Anvil, based on the Ford F-150 Lightning, to demonstrate the unique body panels its metalworking machines could produce. While still fairly crude, this early prototype got Toyota’s attention, and the Japanese automotive giant is now an investor in Machina Labs via Woven Capital, Toyota’s venture capital division.

In a recent development, the process has improved vastly since the Anvil was built, and to demonstrate this, Machina Labs created a upcoming show vehicle, the Lassen, which is being shown at the Los Angeles auto show. Based on a Toyota Tacoma, the Lassen wears a unique hood, tailgate, and fenders, showing off the sort of customization that Machina’s process is capable of. Machina worked with Callum, the design house formed by Ian Callum, to pen the look of these panels before manufacturing them using the RoboCraftsman platform.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405.

While the Lassen isn’t a drastic departure from a standard Tacoma, the changes that Machina made would typically take around four to six months to produce via traditional methods, the manufacturer said at a media event at its second factory in Chatsworth, California. Using its RoboCraftsman platform, Machina was able to take the Lassen from sketches to a finished product in just two and a half weeks.

Sources indicate that the Lassen reveals off Machina’s two main capabilities. The hood and tailgate demonstrate the RoboCraftsman’s ability to re-strike pre-stamped panels with custom designs. The Lassen’s tailgate has a bold embossed Machina script, while the hood also indicates Machina and has a topographical map of its namesake, Mount Lassen in California. The RoboCraftsman platform can put just about any design on a metal panel, and Machina also had tailgates on display featuring a retro Toyota design and a Los Angeles Rams logo.

The fenders, meanwhile, are entirely new panels formed by the RoboCraftsman, and they have a bulging, powerful look. These fenders started as a sheet of metal—Machina works in both aluminum and steel—before being shaped by the robotic arms. This process is a bit slower than the re-striking process, which can take minutes to complete, but a fully formed panel can be finished within hours.

Recent findings suggest that machina believes its RoboCraftsman platform is best suited to production runs in the hundreds and thousands. This could include special-edition models for large OEMs, or working with aftermarket companies to create body kits and other visual customizations. OEMs can also use Machina’s process to swiftly create body panels for early pre-production vehicles, typically an expensive and time-consuming part of the development cycle. In the future, Machina also envisions sending its RoboCraftsman units directly to OEM manufacturing sites to speed up the process even further.

Over the past decade, high-end carmakers realized there is a lot of money in personalization, leading to a surge of one-off and limited-production supercars, designed to the exacting specification desired by their wealthy buyers. These cars, often hand-built, are incredibly expensive. Machina Labs says that its RoboCraftsman platform could democratize customization, with the speed and flexibility at which it can work allowing automakers to save money and offer personalized details on more ordinary, everyday vehicles.

According to recent reports, the RoboCraftsman platform provides a way to quickly manufacture custom body panels, and the flexibility to switch among a large number of different projects in a short amount of time. The Lassen serves as a proof of concept as Machina courts automotive companies, and seeing the RoboCraftsman operate in person, we certainly see a space in the automotive world for Machina’s quick and flexible manufacturing innovation.

Volkswagen’s original microbus became a cultural icon thanks to its open, customizable interior, making it perfect for large families, road trips, camping, and, of course, music festivals.

The ID. Buzz brings the classic Type 2 microbus into the electric era with a retro-fresh style, modern tech, and a flexible, spacious cabin.

Building on its reputation as a symbol of freedom and adventure, Volkswagen is adding a new member to the electric people mover lineup.

Sources indicate that the latest ID. Buzz Beach “brings adventure into the electric age,” Volkswagen mentioned after introducing the new variant on Thursday. Designed for camping, longer road trips, and overnight stays, the electric van will be available in 5-, 6-, and 7-seat configurations.

Volkswagen said it sleeps two comfortably with a removable bed frame and a custom-fitting folding mattress.

The mattress is a decent size at about 6.5 feet long by 4 feet wide (2.0m x 1.2m), roughly the size of an average small double bed.

In the 5-seat configuration, the bed frame tucks away in the trunk, while in the 6- and 7-seat layouts, it’s stored vertically behind the third row of seats.

For camping and other longer stays, Volkswagen added a latest Overnight mode that uses the vehicle’s battery to provide up to 48 hours of continuous, off-grid climate control. The new mode can be accessed on the center touchscreen.

It also includes blackout curtains throughout the cabin and ventilation grilles on the front side windows.

The ID. Buzz Beach offers vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities. A 230V power socket adaptor comes standard, letting you power an e-bike, charge a smartphone, run camping equipment, or power other external electronic devices. A camping connector is available as an added option.

To top it off, Volkswagen added a hidden foldable table and chairs set that can be tucked away without taking up internal space.

According to recent reports, volkswagen will open orders for the newly introduced ID. Buzz Beach in the UK later this month, starting at £53,955 (excluding VAT), or about $71,000. Including VAT and OTR costs, it will start at £65,837, or roughly $86,500.

It has been revealed that nice product at the wrong price. If VW can't lower the price because of the cost, then it has a lot more work to do to compete in this market.

According to recent reports, what about those in the US? VW introduced the 2027 ID. Buzz with a newly introduced Tourer model that was essentially the same as the Beach variant in the UK, with a fold-out mattress, Overnight mode, blackout curtains, and a table and chairs set.

However, VW told its US dealers in September that it would be delaying the ID. Buzz’s return until the 2028 model year.

The 2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz started at about $60,000 in the US, which is one of the biggest reasons it failed to catch on with buyers. The original VW microbus was an affordable people mover.

Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth.
  • William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.
  • “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he indicates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

“The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he indicates. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”.

Industry observers note that astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

Recent findings suggest that “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, noted in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward latest frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

Recent findings suggest that even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

According to recent reports, “Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” notes Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”.

Sources indicate that “Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”.

According to recent reports, voyager 1 debuted on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

Recent findings suggest that as part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

Recent findings suggest that on February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

All good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are currently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical issues, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

Industry observers note that “Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any new region.”.

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an important lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

“Do not be afraid to dream massive. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he states. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”.

UPDATE November 19 10:00 a.m. EST: An earlier version of this story said light moves at 186,282 feet per second. It is 186,282 miles per second. We have updated unit of measurement and apologize for the error.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that toyota has had incredible success with pickup trucks in the United States of America. The Tacoma has become one of America’s perennial best-selling vehicles, while the Tundra has carved out a sustainable niche in America’s grueling full-size segment. But there’s arguably room for more.

Rumors have long suggested Toyota is working on a compact, Ford Maverick-fighting pickup that would fill the truck lineup’s glaring need for a cheaper and more efficient option. Dealers have reportedly been asking Toyota for a compact pickup for several years. Mark Templin, Toyota’s COO in the United States, confirmed Toyota is “looking at” bringing a smaller pickup to the U.S. back in May 2025. And now, Toyota has just unveiled a new pickup that could fit that bill … for Latin American and Caribbean markets.

It has been revealed that toyota revealed a latest compact pickup called the Corolla Cross Deck on Wednesday during its inauguration of a new production facility in Sococaba, Brazil, and it will enter production in the first half of 2027. According to Motor1 Brazil, the Corolla Cross Deck shares a TNGA-C platform with the Corolla sedan and Corolla Cross SUV. Toyota did not provide full specs, but did reveal a hybrid version—likely featuring the 1.8-liter 122-horsepower powertrain Toyota uses for the Corolla Cross in that market.

Sadly, Toyota has not confirmed potential availability for the Corolla Cross Deck in the American market. The automaker did not respond to a Road & Track inquiry about its potential availability by the time of publication, but we’ll update this story if we receive a response.

Recent findings suggest that on paper, a Corolla-based compact pickup would likely be the easiest route for Toyota to bring a small, cheap pickup to the United States in the foreseeable future. Toyota already builds the Corolla and Corolla Cross at its Mazda Toyota Manufacturing Facility in Alabama; a new truck truck could be built on the same line—and even spawn potential rebadged variants for Toyota partners Mazda and Subaru.

In the American market, the Toyota Corolla Cross uses 2.0-liter gas and hybrid engines. That powertrain could give Toyota options for a 169-horsepower base gas model truck—potentially starting below $30,000—and a 196-hp hybrid version that could eclipse 40 miles per gallon.

That mentioned, one could also see Toyota needing a different small truck approach to resonate with an American audience. One of Ford’s great innovations with the Maverick was that it looks more like the F-150 and Ranger than the Escape crossover it shared a platform with. And even if a new Toyota pickup were to share its bones with the Corolla, Toyota may want to brand it as an extension of the pickup line, rather than the Corolla family.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I missed a deadline last week. The piece you’re reading was supposed to be filed before I headed out on a long weekend to Italy for my wife’s birthday.

The main problem was I simply ran out of time to write the piece. An urgent stakeholder ask out of the blue, a couple of unanticipated work fire drills, and a long-standing evening social commitment earlier in the week made for a perfect storm, and something had to give.

The other problem and consequence was that I carried a chunk of guilt into the break.

It caught up with me at 6 am on the first morning, when I found myself drafting this column in my head. I should have been dozing peacefully. I continued to ruminate on my lengthy to-do list at work deep into day one as we headed from Venice into the Dolomites. My body was in Italy, but my brain was clearly still at my desk.

Industry observers note that switching off, particularly from work, is hard for most of us, and especially in an age of ubiquitous screens and wall-to-wall information competing for our attention. For me, that always-on reality plays a major role in the difficulties I have disconnecting from the daily grind.

I’m fortunate to love my job, and if I’m candid, I probably take a little too much of my identity from it. I hold on tight, and the phone in my pocket is an ever-present enabler.

A meme that has stuck with me over the years goes something along the lines of being an adult is staring at medium screens all day only to come home and stare at a little screen while a significant screen is on in the background. The irony is not lost on me that I came across this rather withering take on modern life while scrolling on mentioned little screen.

According to recent reports, regardless of the role the screen plays, psychologists who study employee well-being describe what I was missing for the early part of the weekend as “psychological detachment.” A state where you are genuinely able to not think about work while away from it. The science suggests it’s an important thing to work on.

It has been revealed that A 2025 meta-analysis of 32 studies found that vacationing has a strong effect on well-being, and that the effect lasts longer than earlier research suggested. A second, smaller analysis of eight studies points to detaching from work, along with physical activity, as among the most helpful things to do while you’re off. In another study that tracked teachers during a two-week break, exhaustion, anxiety, and low mood all declined, while those who kept ruminating about work recovered less.

Whatever the science says, I know that for me the act of stepping away from work and being disciplined about not checking back in while I’m away is critical for my mental health and for staving off burnout. Getting out in nature and hiking or cycling or swimming keeps me present. It resets and recharges my batteries, and it tops up my creativity in a way that I find benefits what I am then able to bring back to the office.

Sure enough, as we drove deeper into the mountains on a crisp, blue-sky day, I could feel the golden autumnal hues and majestic rock formations drawing me in, closer to an elemental feeling of calm and happiness. That sense of equilibrium stayed with me all weekend, and while I’d be lying if I noted my mind didn’t occasionally drift to my desk, it was fleeting, with the knowledge that all the things would be waiting for me when I got back. Just like this piece was.

In a recent development, with Thanksgiving on the horizon, and the holidays coming thick and fast thereafter, I’ll leave you with this bit of hard-earned advice: if your job is deeply entwined with your life and part of who you are, as mine is, time away can sometimes feel like a small act of disloyalty. It isn’t. In fact, it’s probably the most key thing you can do to remain faithful to your work ethic, and to yourself.

And if you’ll be working over the holidays, or you’re not working right now, or you don’t have the benefit of someone on hand to carry some of the load for you (shout out to all the Grannies out there), or your vacation looks very different from mine, that’s all okay. Find the pockets where and when you can: an evening, a walk, an hour in front of a screen, or better yet a book, and let work wait. Above all else, be kind to yourself. That’s how you really give yourself a break.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

Breaking: Boost and Booster Seats: Comparing the Turbocharged 2026 VW Tiguan and Mazda CX-50

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the horsepower wars are not relegated to machines purpose-built for performance.
  • Of course, building a holistically satisfying family car involves more than just adding power.
  • Both models here—the Tiguan SEL R-Line and the CX-50 Premium Plus—represent the pinnacle of their lineups and are thus quite expensive as far as small family SUVs go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the horsepower wars are not relegated to machines purpose-built for performance. Nowadays, it feels like nearly every automaker has some sort of higher-output solution available across a surprisingly wide swath of its fleet, including seemingly pedestrian family vehicles. Some might come via electrification, but in the case of the two vehicles before us today—the 2026 Volkswagen Tiguan and 2026 Mazda CX-50—these hi-po conveyances twist the asphalt with good old-fashioned gasoline and turbochargers.

Of course, building a holistically satisfying family car involves more than just adding power. Extra oomph might satisfy the driver, but automakers must pay attention to a whole host of other factors to make things just as peachy for the passengers. Let’s see which of these two compact SUVs does just that.

Both models here—the Tiguan SEL R-Line and the CX-50 Premium Plus—represent the pinnacle of their lineups and are thus quite expensive as far as small family SUVs go. The Tiguan’s lineup starts at $32,280 for the S, and our tester bookends the other side of the offerings at $46,170 as tested. The CX-50 is less expensive, starting at $31,395 for the Select model; our range-topper’s window sticker came in slightly more affordable than the VW’s at $45,210.

See all results for latest 2026 Mazda CX-50 for sale near 47240.

Neither of these vehicles is a screaming deal, but you can save a bit of scratch on the VW. Skip our car’s $850 Avocado Green paint, $405 auto-dimming rearview mirror, and $365 in floor mats and bumper protectors, and the price delta evens out. Our Mazda’s Cypress Green paint was only $200 by comparison; all-weather floor mats and a cargo liner added another $390 to its bottom line.

In a recent development, since both models are the top of their pops, you get a stout list of features. The CX-50’s Premium Plus niceties include a surround-view camera, auto-dimming inside and side-view mirrors, rear automatic braking, and blind-spot monitoring. The Tiguan SEL R-Line takes things a step further with massaging front seats (something Mazda doesn’t offer on any vehicle it sells), plus a more aggressive R-Line appearance package that deletes most of the brightwork around the windows and front fascia.

Looks can be deceiving. The Tiguan’s boxy form may appear larger in all dimensions, but it exceeds the Mazda only in overall width (by nearly four inches, including mirrors) and height (by two to three inches). The CX-50 has about an inch more overall length, wheelbase, and ride height.

According to recent reports, slip inside, and the CX-50 puts more stock in front legroom, where it beats the Tiguan, but the Mazda’s rear passengers must make do with fractionally less gam space. Owing in part to its more upright body shape, the Tiguan takes the cargo-capacity crown, offering better volume whether the rear seats are up or down.

See all results for upcoming 2026 Mazda CX-50 for sale near 47240.

It has been revealed that when it comes to cabin aesthetics, both are swinging for the fences. The CX-50’s white-on-black interior carries plush touch points and premium materials, and we love how many physical buttons, dials, and switches exist across nearly every surface. The tucked-away infotainment screen feels like a vestige of an earlier age, and it sort of is—the CX-50 is due for an update that brings it in line with the latest CX-5, for better or worse (read our latest long-term CX-5 update for more on that).

HIGHS: More guts than the average canopic jar, superb bump suppression, feels fancy.LOWS: Creature-comfort corner cutting, tighter rear-seat accommodations, not a highway-fuel-economy hero.VERDICT: A rocket that could use more pockets.

The Tiguan’s cabin is also top-notch. Our tester’s two-tone brown and black interior looks and feels no less luxurious than an Audi’s, and we enjoyed the door-to-door strip of wood, which adds some extra variety. Of course, the latest-gen Tiguan is all about the screens, which in this case comprise a normal digital gauge display and a 15-inch repurposed highway billboard. In addition to having more cargo capacity, the Tiguan also has more places to stash your stuff.

In a recent development, we have one weird thing to point out, but it’s bound to be key to somebody. Both cars have heated steering wheels, but the Mazda’s heating element seems confined to between 9 and 10 o’clock on the left and between 2 and 3 o’clock on the right, while the rest of the tiller remains icy to the touch. Volkswagen’s engineers, on the other hand, smartly realized that if you pay for a heated steering wheel, you probably want one that’s warm the whole way around.

Recent findings suggest that even among high-strung turbo fours, the No Replacement for Displacement adage still holds true. The Mazda CX-50’s 256-hp turbocharged 2.5-liter makes less horsepower than the Tiguan, but the larger mill churns out an absurd 320 pound-feet of torque. All-wheel drive is standard, as is an archaic six-speed automatic transmission. The CX-50 is the lightweight here, tipping the scales at 3864 pounds.

Recent findings suggest that by comparison, the Tiguan’s 2.0-liter turbo four makes just 258 pound-feet of torque, but at 268 horses, it bests the Mazda on raw horsepower. All-wheel drive is standard here as well, and the transmission is a more modern-feeling eight-speed auto. The whole Teutonic shebang carries about one more human’s worth of mass in its structure, weighing 4023 pounds on our scales.

Industry observers note that if you’re assuming that the lighter, more torquey SUV will outperform its competition, you’re right, but the gap is small. The last CX-50 we tested hustles to 60 mph in 6.4 seconds—two-tenths ahead of the Tiguan—and the Mazda’s 167-foot stop from 70 mph bests the VW by nine feet. From there, things really tighten up: The CX-50’s 14.9-second, 92-mph quarter-mile sprint is just a hair ahead of the Tiguan’s 15.0 seconds at 96 mph. With a 5-mph rolling start, the two reach 60 within a tenth of each other. From 50 to 70, the Vee-Dub takes the lead, requiring just 4.5 seconds to the Mazda’s 4.8. The Mazda notches a victory around the skidpad, maintaining 0.84 g of lateral grip against the Volkswagen’s 0.78 g.

HIGHS: Posh cabin trimmings, slightly more spacious inside, the most fun we’ve had in a VW SUV in a while.LOWS: Not our favorite infotainment interface, not our favorite brake pedal, traditional German road compliance.VERDICT: Fun for the whole family, driver included.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, the CX-50’s lighter curb weight and slicker-looking silhouette don’t translate to stonkin’ fuel-economy benefits. The two vehicles are nearly evenly matched by EPA estimates—both earned 29-mpg highway and 25-mpg combined ratings, but the Mazda’s 23-mpg city value tops the VW’s by one. The script flipped on our real-world 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, however, where the Tiguan overachieved with a 31-mpg result, out-skinflinting the 28-mpg Mazda, which fell short of its EPA highway estimate.

Both SUVs are fun to drive and reward time spent behind the wheel, with each vehicle carrying its own little idiosyncrasies. There are a few parts of the driving experience where we think the CX-50 shines, and others where the Tiguan feels better.

The Mazda’s cabin may be louder at wide-open throttle (and tied at a 70-mph cruise), but overall, it seems quieter in day-to-day operation, especially over the zydeco washboards that Ann Arbor calls roads. The CX-50’s bump damping is superior, making for a slightly more luxurious ride quality than the Tiguan, which carries some of that stereotypical German stiffness in its suspension tuning—but one person’s “flinty” is another person’s “composed,” so it really boils down to whether you want that additional poise in your daily driving. (The Tiguan SE and base S offer smaller wheels with cushier tire sidewalls.).

When it comes to pedal feel, the Mazda takes the crown; the Tiguan’s brake pedal is a little mushy, and the throttle is a little too eager to open ’er up with a gentle tip-in. On the other hand, we preferred the Volkswagen’s heftier steering feel. The Mazda’s six-speed automatic handles gear changes deftly, but it’s clear from our on-ramp-style acceleration testing that the VW’s two extra gears are, in fact, providing a benefit. (Highway fuel-economy results reflect that as well.) It’s not like you’ll notice either gearbox doing its job, though.

By the skin of its teeth, the Volkswagen Tiguan claims the championship belt that it lost to the Mazda CX-50 in a 2024 two-car comparo. Back then, we noted the CX-50 was worth the upcharge over the more efficient, more spacious Volkswagen because we preferred the Mazda’s cabin and driving dynamics.

Now, the Tiguan is the one that costs more, and while it remains more efficient and more spacious than the CX-50, it picked up some major slack in the interior-design department, and it drives just about as well. The 2026 Tiguan is an excellent all-rounder. It’s a wonder what a new generation can do.

#109644. BYD’s folding steering wheel isn’t a concept — it’s in a $49K SUV now

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1135 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

BYD’s folding steering wheel isn’t a concept — it’s in a $49K SUV now

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, BYD launched a production SUV today with a steering wheel that folds flat into the dashboard.
  • Automakers and suppliers have been parading folding wheels on concept cars for about a decade.
  • Recent findings suggest that the whole thing hinges on steer-by-wire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, BYD launched a production SUV today with a steering wheel that folds flat into the dashboard. It comes standard on the top trim of the Fang Cheng Bao Tai 9, which sells for 329,900 yuan (about $49,000) in China.

Automakers and suppliers have been parading folding wheels on concept cars for about a decade. This is the first one customers can actually order, according to BYD.

Recent findings suggest that the whole thing hinges on steer-by-wire. There’s no steering column physically connecting the wheel to the front wheels, so the wheel is just an input device, and BYD can put it wherever it wants.

On the Tai 9, it swings through 180 degrees on a hidden hinge and drops into a compartment in the dash in about 10 seconds. A panel closes over it, and a tray table folds out where the wheel used to be. Only the airbag remains outside of the compartment – keeping it useful with the steering wheel deployed or hidden.

Sources indicate that it only folds when the vehicle is parked. Fang Cheng Bao pairs it with a driver’s seat that reclines to 165 degrees, so the pitch is simple: fold the wheel, lie back, and eat, nap, or play games while you charge or wait. The brand claims 80% of the driver’s area becomes usable space and rates the folding mechanism for 80,000 cycles.

Recent findings suggest that when it’s deployed, it’s a regular D-shaped wheel with a full rim and physical buttons. No yoke. That’s a nice change from Tesla and Mercedes, which paired its new steer-by-wire system on the EQS with a yoke.

It has been revealed that at the launch event, Fang Cheng Bao general manager Xiong Tianbo said the industry had been talking about folding steering wheels since 2016 without ever getting one into mass production. He added that BYD is using the same type of motor it develops for humanoid robots to move the wheel, a first in one of its cars.

Here’s Fang Cheng Bao’s official video of the feature:.

China’s new national standard for steering systems took effect on July 1, 2026. It dropped the long-standing requirement for a mechanical link between the steering wheel and the road wheels, as long as the system meets redundancy and fail-safe rules.

In a recent development, before that, steer-by-wire needed special approval. Nio’s ET9 was the first car in China to get it, back in December 2024. In the US, Tesla’s Cybertruck already uses it, and Mercedes is bringing it to the EQS this year.

Folding wheels themselves have stayed on show stands. BYD’s own Denza brand showed one on the Z concept at Shanghai in 2025. Autoliv and Tensor called theirs the “world’s first foldable steering wheel” at CES in January, for a Tensor Robocar they expected to reach volume production in the second half of 2026. Hyundai Mobis has been showing one for years.

Tesla went the other way with the Cybercab: no wheel at all. But the prototypes testing on public roads have a Cybertruck steering wheel bolted onto an exposed column, because a human still has to be able to drive.

The Tai 9 is Fang Cheng Bao’s biggest SUV yet. It’s 5,270 mm (207.5 in) long with a 3,130 mm wheelbase and six seats in a 2+2+2 layout. It’s also the first model on BYD’s upcoming DMS hybrid platform.

It has been revealed that A 1.5-liter turbo engine works with front and rear electric motors for a combined 400 kW (536 hp), and 0 to 100 km/h takes 4.8 seconds. The 66.48 kWh second-generation Blade battery supports BYD’s flash charging and delivers 310 km (193 miles) of electric range on the WLTC cycle. Rear-wheel steering, LiDAR, and BYD’s God’s Eye B driver assistance system are standard.

There are three trims: 279,900 yuan (about $41,700), 299,900 yuan, and 329,900 yuan. Only the top one gets the folding wheel.

According to recent reports, fang Cheng Bao sold 43,872 vehicles in October, up 41% year-over-year, mostly on the strength of the Tai 7. That model is now heading overseas: BYD sells it in the UK as the Ti 7. BYD hasn’t remarked anything about exporting the Tai 9.

It is not only that these technologies are impressive, but it is the speed at which they are being put into market by some of these Chinese car companies like BYD. They are moving further and further away from the competition but its understandable with the insane competition between car makers in China that they almost have to maintain and edge.

Sources indicate that we’ve seen this at pretty much every auto show since the mid-2010s: a steering wheel slides away so the “driver” can relax while the car drives itself. It never shipped, for many reasons, but with steer-by-wire and autonomous driving now becoming reality, BYD is making the jump.

The Tai 9’s wheel only folds when you’re parked, so right now it’s a lounge feature. Recline the seat, stow the wheel, flip out the tray, and watch a movie while you charge. Is that a gimmick? A little. But Chinese EV buyers spend a lot of time in parked cars, and fridges, screens, and lie-flat seats sell cars there for a reason.

The bigger deal is underneath. The wheel can only fold because the Tai 9 is steer-by-wire, and BYD is putting that in a roughly $49,000 family SUV less than five months after China made it legal. After Cybertruck and now Mercedes with the EQS, we might be seeing the first steps of steer-by-wire actually becoming a more widely adopted technology.

#109643. Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (581 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out.
  • Industry observers note that plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury.
  • Environmental biologists certainly did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Industry observers note that plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

Environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a newly introduced, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

“It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, said in a statement.

Wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

Industry observers note that the idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s electric SUVs are getting some love. The IONIQ 5 and three-row IONIQ 9 helped the Korean automaker land its first-ever “Best Electric Vehicle Brand” award from US News & World Report for 2027.

“This win showcases the breadth and strength of Hyundai’s SUV and electric lineups,” Alex Kwanten, managing editor at Autos at US News, noted after naming it the Best EV Brand and Best SUV Brand for 2027.

This marks the first time Hyundai has earned the Best EV Brand award and the third consecutive win for Best SUV Brand.

Including hybrid and electric vehicles, Hyundai offers ten unique SUVs, “many of them at or near the top of our rankings in those classes for capability, comfort, performance and value,” Kwanten stated.

Hyundai’s fully electric SUVs, the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9, “in particular, stand out for their combination of style and technology,” he explained.

Hyundai at the moment offers the IONIQ 5, including the sporty IONIQ 5 N and off-road-focused IONIQ 5 XRT, plus the three-row IONIQ 9.

Although Hyundai discontinued its electric sedan, the IONIQ 6, after the 2025 model year, the newly introduced high-performance IONIQ 6 N joins the lineup in 2027.

Industry observers note that the IONIQ 5 continued to earn praise, taking its third consecutive Best Compact Electric SUV award. Its larger sibling, the IONIQ 9, took the top spot in the midsize electric SUV category.

Hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in the US this year through September that isn’t a Tesla, ranking third behind the Model Y and Model 3.

Why does it continue winning over buyers? The IONIQ 5 checks all the boxes with long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior with modern tech.

It’s also among the most affordable EVs in the US. Prices for the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 start at just $35,250.

Sources indicate that however, the base price is for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model costs an extra $2,500, with prices starting at $37,750, but it offers up to 318 miles of range.

The three-row Hyundai IONIQ 9 electric SUV starts at $58,955 with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles.

According to recent reports, hyundai’s IONIQ 5 is about the size of a Tesla Model Y, with two rows of seating and space for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating with six- or seven-seat options.

The larger IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with up to 106.5 cubic feet in the IONIQ 5.

Both electric SUVs use an 800-volt electrical architecture for ultra-fast charging. The IONIQ 5 can charge from 10% to 80% in about 20 minutes, while the IONIQ 9 takes around 24 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Hyundai assembles the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told Electrek that its electric SUVs are winning over fresh buyers at a higher rate than any of its gas or hybrid vehicles.

Sources indicate that the IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

Is Hyundai the best Electric Vehicle brand in your opinion? While Hyundai took the top spot overall, Lucid remained the Best Luxury EV Brand for the second consecutive year. Hyundai’s Genesis also repeated as Best Luxury Brand. Share your thoughts in the comments below.

A fresh Arc Raiders patch has arrived, bringing a host of fresh fixes to several exploits players have recently been relying on to do things they’re not supposed to, and bypass certain mechanics to get into areas without having to go through proper channels.

The patch is fairly small, and surprisingly doesn’t include any buffs or nerfs to anything in particular.

In a recent development, the list of notes for patch 1.4.0 is compact, with a clear focus on addressing several exploits. The biggest one, of course, is the addition of “exploit mitigation mechanisms” to stop players from glitching through locked doors.

It has been revealed that this fix applies to all maps, and it’s intended to address an issue whereby players would not bring the required keys to access those areas of the various maps. Locked rooms, if they can be unlocked, often hide a wealth of high-tier and rare loot.

But players have also been using similar exploits to clip through walls and access areas outside the playspace, allowing them to ambush enemy players and set up traps that would be impossible for others to detect.

According to recent reports, the game’s recent patch, which was released exactly one week ago, mainly consisted of balance tweaks to some of the more popular weapons and mines. However, it also introduced a few fixes to prevent players from clipping through walls by using barricades.

While on the subject of being in places where you’re not supposed to, the patch blocked exterior access to the locked room inside Spaceport's Control Tower, making it only accessible from inside the tower.

1.4.0 also fixes an especially nasty exploit that allowed players to bring up their weapons much faster than normal by swiftly swapping to the quick use menu. There’s a range of smaller fixes for lighting and texture bugs here, too, and you can read all about it in the full change log below:.
