📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In what has come to feel like the dawn of the final day before Grand Theft Auto VI's release, one thing that Rockstar really don't want people to be aware of is the ongoing legal dispute between the Rockstar Games Workers Union and the studio itself following Rockstar's alleged union busting in firing 31 union members last year. Starting on the 12th through to the 26th, recognition of the union will be voted upon by staff to ensure that workers would be given a say over "topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies.".

Sources indicate that if it passes, the vote would also make the union the largest recognised union in the UK games industry, partly thanks to its partnership with the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain. Now, the global labor union SAG-AFTRA have chimed in to endorse the Workers Union, offering solidarity to the members involved and granting important leverage from a global force.

SAG-AFTRA's statement declares that "unionisation is vital for the future of the video game industry", and that "in the face of record layoffs, job instability, hostile work places, and toxic crunch culture, it is now more critical than ever for unions and workers to stand in support of one another." They advocate for fair treatment, especially in the wake of displacement due to corporate mismanagement and genAI, and proudly state that "this is a fight for all workers.".

Their statement closes by saying that "the gaming industry is a commercial juggernaut, and the people that create these amazing works of art deserve fair treatment and the opportunity to improve the terms of their employment with a strong voice at the bargaining table. We honor the courage of our fellow game workers at Rockstar and proudly support their union vote.".

Solidarity with the workers, always. We can only wait and see how the voting process pans out.

#109480. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1020 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker.
  • According to recent reports, void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand.
  • Industry observers note that this narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

According to recent reports, void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find newly introduced exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

Industry observers note that this narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”.

It has been revealed that the game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

In a recent development, between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as upcoming types are introduced in each stage.

In a recent development, the rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

Sources indicate that bad signal or dead zones? Download your challenges before you leave and read anywhere.

In a press release coinciding with Grand Theft Auto VI becoming available for pre-load ahead of its November 19th release date, Rockstar has confirmed that the game "has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits." Read between the lines, and you can kind of make out the words "...so hope your PCs are up to spec, computer nerds.".

GTA 6, of course, still does not have a confirmed PC version, even if Rockstar's former tech director says it's probably not far off. And despite this, even ancient, last-gen consoles are getting in on it, as the release also unexpectedly confirms that the game will be playable on Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming, Microsoft's game streaming service that has suddenly lost its ability to work on PC. Granted, this comes with a warning: "as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay." If you ended up getting a PS4 last generation, no cloud play for you either, I'm afraid. It also states that it will "play best on Playstation 5 consoles", making great use of that Sony partnership, and will include Playstation Spectral Super Resolution and ray-traced shadows on PS5 Pro.

A 2026 current-gen game targeting 30fps, let alone one as titanic of a release as GTA VI, is probably not going to go down well with a lot of people, even if console players are traditionally les sensitive about FPS counts than PC players. What this does imply, though, is that the inevitable PC release might be an even more demanding behemoth than expected, if Xbox Series and PS5 versions can't even target 60fps. The availability of the game on Xbox One, even if just through cloud streaming, could have resulted in an acceptance that 60fps just wasn't going to be possible if it was also going to be able to 'run' on last-gen hardware. Either way, when it does eventually escape console exclusivity, hopefully trying to run GTA VI on anything less than an RTX 5080 won't set your PC on fire. Now, let me just swiftly have a glance at GPU prices. Oh, no.

#109477. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1189 w)

Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An international research team has developed a latest technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease.
  • Recent findings suggest that the technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain.
  • Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An international research team has developed a latest technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

Recent findings suggest that the technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the latest approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

Sources indicate that for some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

Recent findings suggest that "The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers.".

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells.

The newly introduced technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces.".

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

Recent findings suggest that "The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she indicates. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain.".

In a recent development, the process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice.

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

In a recent development, "Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an key target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.".

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly key because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

It has been revealed that after the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice demonstrated significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

According to recent reports, however, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

According to recent reports, one possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

Recent findings suggest that "Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately.".

Industry observers note that beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a newly introduced way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward latest approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, since its release earlier this year, Hell Let Loose: Vietnam has gotten plenty of praise for capturing the grit and horrors of the jungles of Vietnam. At the same time, the game has also been on the receiving end of criticism for its rather limited arsenal.

The dev team over at Expression Games has taken that to heart. After addressing the two more glaring omissions by adding the American M14 and the Soviet SKS, the most iconic Western weapon of the Cold War is finally making its way to Southeast Asia.

The next big release for Hell Let Loose: Vietnam, update 2.0, is bringing the FN FAL into the fray, specifically in its British version that saw combat in the region.

Introduced in 1953, the FAL holds the distinction of being the first modern service rifle to enter widespread service in the West.

Recent findings suggest that chambered for the same 7.62x51mm NATO as the M14, M40 and M60 already in the game, the L1A1 SLR (Self-Loading Rifle) variant comes with a 20-round box magazine and is limited to semi-automatic fire. This was a design choice by Commonwealth clients, and really, unless you want to shoot down NVA planes while aiming at the horizon, you won’t notice the difference.

In Hell Let Loose: Vietnam, the L1A1 will be available to the United States & Allies faction to represent its service with Australian and Newly introduced Zealander units deployed there. Unlike the M14, the new rifle won’t be available to the Rifleman role.

The FAL holds the distinction of being the first modern service rifle to enter widespread service in the West.

To use the L1A1, you’ll need to reach level 6 in one of the following roles:.

Recent findings suggest that I want to caveat here that if you actually pick the L1A1 over the M60 while playing machine gunner, you are a bad person and your team will be short in firepower. MG roles are for pouring it on downrange, not for reloading after twenty shots, and I’m saying this as a staunch FAL defender.

The developers have not offered any insight on how the pilots are supposed to fit a rifle that long in the cockpit of the Huey, but we can look the other way for a little bit.

As much as I’m pining for the L1A1 and it will be my personal highlight of update 2.0 for Hell Let Loose: Vietnam, it’s hard to argue against the real big item on the prospective patch notes being the Khe Sanh map and what it means for the game as a whole.

Khe Sanh will be the debut map for the Assault game mode, doubling down on the attackers versus defenders gameplay already present in the Offensive mode.

Assault brings back a fan favorite from the World War 2 Hell Let Loose, and focuses specifically on horrific trench warfare, strongpoints, and choosing whether you prefer dying in a fatal funnel in a trench or getting ripped apart by artillery out in the open. It’s great fun once you get used to the tinnitus.

Level designer Kienan Suthar provides more detail in this deep dive:.

The battle of Khe Sanh was one of the toughest battles in the Vietnam War, coinciding with the Tet Offensive of January 1968 and lasting until July of that same year.

In a recent development, khe Sanh Combat Base was surrounded by a large North Vietnamese force, supported by Viet Cong and Pathet Lao rebels. For five months, US and allied forces reinforced the base primarily from the air, while throwing everything and the kitchen sink at the Vietnamese troops.

According to recent reports, the outcome of the battle, as many major engagements of the Vietnam War, was inconclusive. The North Vietnamese siege was partially lifted by April 1968, but a shift in US strategy in the aftermath of the Tet Offensive led to its abandonment on July 9.

According to recent reports, for the Americans, avoiding a Điện Biên Phủ situation and preventing the collapse of the base was considered a win. The North Vietnamese, meanwhile, celebrated victory by capturing the region following the withdrawal.

For players, the real tangible outcome is that it created an incredibly dense network of fortifications for Hell Let Loose: Vietnam to sink its teeth into the assault mode.

Update 2.0 for Hell Let Loose: Vietnam is scheduled for the first half of December. Hell Let Loose: Vietnam is currently available on PC, PlayStation 5, and XBOX Series X/S.

The Red Bull Formula 1 team has a brutal reputation for chewing up promising new drivers, but Kiwi driver Liam Lawson has kept his focus after being demoted from being Max Verstappen’s teammate back to the junior Visa Cash App Racing Bulls (VCARB) team in 2025. Lawson had an excellent year with the Racing Bulls so far, including a top-10 finish and a respectable stand-in back at Red Bull over the summer filling in for an injured Isack Hadjar.

In a recent development, despite his performance, he was unsure of his seat for 2027 until just a few days ago, when VCARB confirmed Lawson and teammate Arvid Lindblad will both return for next year. Discussion of the future was still off limits for this interview, but it was a noticeably relaxed Liam Lawson who sat down with us to talk about massive trucks, sad songs, and what makes Vegas such a tough race.

Car and Driver: What is the week leading up to a race like, especially a media-heavy one like Las Vegas?

See all results for used cars for sale near 80222.

Industry observers note that liam Lawson: Vegas is a unique race in many aspects. The timings of it [Vegas is a night race]. And then this weekend for us, this year in general with these cars, there were fresh regulations, new power units. Every weekend has been a bit of a challenge to learn. Vegas is very cold and not high grip, it's very, very low grip. The track’s quite dirty as well. They open the street up at night and it sort of makes it quite difficult for us when we come back the next day. So the prep that goes in is a little bit more than normal. We’re definitely doing a lot on the simulator side.

Do you guys have a way to do simulator work on the road, not just sort of between races?

Industry observers note that oh, no, unfortunately not. It’s back at base Milton Keynes. So for a triple header like this [Vegas, Qatar, Abu Dhabi], we will do time on all three tracks before and get them basically dialed and then go to the races, but we don’t have time to go back in between races, unfortunately.

I guess I hadn’t really thought of it that way, but because the setup is so different, even tracks that you’re very familiar with are going to be almost like upcoming tracks. Like each race you’re all running for the first time with this setup.

Sources indicate that yeah, it’s very different, especially at the start of the year. I would say things are now getting a lot more consistent as we get in the groove of things. It's been tricky and we’ve just been learning through the year and the cars have been getting a lot better as well as we bring upgrades. It’s been a lot busier. We started probably in January, a lot earlier than normal with preseason testing and trying to get a handle on these cars.

It has been revealed that you’re known as a pretty technical guy, a pretty technical driver. What’s your relationship with your team in terms of giving them feedback on the cars or being involved in setup?

I think it’s crucial the relationship you have with your engineers, that they understand the type of driver that you are as well, because, the way that you give feedback sometimes can be misheard, you know, or like misunderstood. My relationship with the guys I work with has strengthened a lot through the year. Alex [race engineer Alexandre Iliopoulos], when I’m speaking about something, he knows pretty much what I’m saying and understands it.

I talk about what I feel in the car and report that back. And then I talk about the main things that I need from the car to be quicker in the next sessions.

Recent findings suggest that you sound very comfortable with that. Another crucial part of your guys’ job, especially in the last few years as F1 has become so much more mainstream, is social media. How do you like that kind of stuff? How do you deal with it? Do you think it’s fun? Do you hate it?

Oh let’s talk about that! You’re a musician as well as a driver.

Guitar. That’s something I’ve done since I was very young. My parents had me playing and learning classical guitar. Now I just play for fun, mostly like country music.

Yeah, mostly motocross. The track I have at home, it’s not too crazy. It’s on the safer side, you know, I would say it doesn’t have any like crazy doubles or stuff.

Like a sleeper agent activated late in the game, Elana Scherr didn’t know her calling at a young age. Like many girls, she planned to be a vet-astronaut-artist, and came closest to that last one by attending UCLA art school. She painted images of cars, but did not own one. Elana reluctantly got a driver’s license at age 21 and discovered that she not only loved cars and wanted to drive them, but that other people loved cars and wanted to read about them, which meant somebody had to write about them. Since receiving activation codes, Elana has written for numerous car magazines and websites, covering classics, car culture, technology, motorsports, and new-car reviews. In 2020, she received a Best Feature award from the Motor Press Guild for the C/D story "A Drive through Classic Americana in a Polestar 2."  In 2023, her Car and Driver feature story "In Washington, D.C.'s Secret Carpool Cabal, It's a Daily Slug Fest" was awarded 1st place in the 16th Annual National Arts & Entertainment Journalism Awards by the Los Angeles Press Club.

Recent findings suggest that as another addition to the slew of smaller studios being dissolved by their parent companies, Bandai Namco announced in a press release that they are shutting down their subsidiary studio Reflector Entertainment, a Montreal studio responsible for 2024's action-adventure game Unknown 9: Awakening. In its notice, Bandai Namco explains that the reason for the liquidation is due to Reflector not meeting its expectations for "future business prepares, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation.".

The press release notes that the liquidation of Reflector will result in an estimated "extraordinary loss" of around 21 million euros, or 3.5 billion yen, for Bandai Namco in its Q3 fiscal report of this year. This is not the first time Reflector has been cut by Bandai, as around a month after the launch of Unknown 9: Awakening and presumably in response to its low sales, 18% of the workforce was laid off. 2025 then saw further redundancies amidst the cancellation of a prospective project, though details on those layoffs were not granted by the organization. Unknown 9 was intended to be a transmedia franchise involving the game as well as comic books and novels, but these ambitions never came to pass.

Industry observers note that bandai Namco notes that the liquidation will be held to local laws and procedures, which make the actual schedule of the process uncertain for now. A similar process faces Arkane Lyon, which is currently in a purgatory of having been chosen for closure by Microsoft, but temporarily protected by French labor laws that prevent it from being suddenly closed without proper negotiation and procedure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead unveiled a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios stated that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Sources indicate that escalating the fight with upcoming threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj.

It has been revealed that what we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension patch is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

According to recent reports, similar to other Bonus Paths, the new Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several newly introduced customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

10 Games to Play If You Loved Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are few things worse than finishing a fantastic adventure and realizing you have no idea what to play next.
  • Sources indicate that after spending hours exploring Hyrule, solving puzzles, and facing some of gaming's most memorable bosses, it's only natural to feel a little lost when the credits finally roll.
  • While no game can truly replace the feeling of playing Ocarina of Time for the first time, there are plenty of experiences out there that capture some of the same magic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are few things worse than finishing a fantastic adventure and realizing you have no idea what to play next. With The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake arriving earlier this month, plenty of players are probably reaching that bittersweet moment already!

Sources indicate that after spending hours exploring Hyrule, solving puzzles, and facing some of gaming's most memorable bosses, it's only natural to feel a little lost when the credits finally roll. But don't worry, because I'm here to help you find your next adventure.

While no game can truly replace the feeling of playing Ocarina of Time for the first time, there are plenty of experiences out there that capture some of the same magic. Whether it's a mysterious world waiting to be explored, clever dungeons, unforgettable characters, or a story that stays with you long after you've put the controller down, there's something on this list for every kind of Zelda fan.

So, if you're already missing Hyrule and aren't quite ready to say goodbye to that feeling of adventure, here are 10 games worth checking out. Some might remind you of classic Zelda, while others take those familiar ideas in completely different directions. Either way, I think you'll find something worth getting lost in!

In a recent development, nothing beats dealing with the sadness of finishing a fantastic game by jumping straight into its sequel, right? That's why we're kicking things off with Majora's Mask, the final Zelda entry released on the Nintendo 64 and one of the darkest adventures in the entire franchise.

Industry observers note that although it reuses plenty of assets and the basic gameplay of Ocarina of Time, Majora's has an entirely different atmosphere. There's no Triforce, no Princess Zelda to rescue, and no Ganondorf plotting to take over Hyrule. Instead, a mysterious moon is about to crash into the town of Termina, and Link happens to have his Ocarina stolen by the mischievous creature responsible for the whole mess – then, well, someone has to save the day!

This leads to one of the most fascinating mechanics in the series: a three-day time loop that has you traveling through time, helping eccentric characters, and learning the daily schedules of the town's residents. Interestingly, the Ocarina of Time remake actually brings a little more of that NPC schedule system into its own villages, making this sequel feel like a particularly natural follow-up.

If you love the combination of dungeons, memorable boss fights, unusual mechanics, and, of course, a lovely talking companion, then Okami should be right up your alley.

With a structure heavily inspired by classic Zelda adventures, this is one of Capcom's most beloved games, and its story draws heavily from Japanese folklore, following Amaterasu, the sun goddess who takes the form of a white wolf. She must restore life to a land plagued by an ancient evil, beginning with a legendary eight-headed demon that was sealed away a hundred years earlier. Gods, broken seals, spirits, and a spreading darkness? Yeah, I think that should ring a bell for anyone familiar with Hyrule.

It's a perfect pick if you're craving another Zelda-like adventure, and the upcoming sequel gives you one more reason to fall in love with this world.

Mina the Hollower takes place in a world filled with talking skeletons and every kind of magical fantasy you can imagine. So, if the Ocarina of Time left you craving another adventure packed with charming characters and a wonderfully imaginative world, this little indie game might be exactly what you're looking for.

This is a 2D action-adventure with roots deeply tied to some of the most iconic games in the genre – and yes, The Legend of Zelda is definitely one of its biggest inspirations. Between its top-down perspective, exploration, combat, and dungeon-like challenges, you'll probably catch some familiar vibes from the original Zelda and A Link to the Past along the way.

What I particularly love, though, is how Mina the Hollower manages to feel like a love letter to those classics without simply copying them. Its unique story and charming gothic aesthetic give it an identity of its own.

If one of the things that stayed with you after playing Ocarina of Time was its bittersweet take on growing up and letting go of the past, then Shadow of the Colossus is an excellent next stop.

Recent findings suggest that this is a much quieter and more melancholic adventure, but it shares that ability to make you feel like you're part of something much bigger than yourself. Instead of exploring villages and dungeons, you'll travel across an enormous, almost deserted landscape on horseback, searching for sixteen colossal creatures. And each encounter is essentially a puzzle of its own, requiring you to figure out how to climb these mysterious beings and find their weak points before delivering the final blow.

According to recent reports, and trust me, there's something incredibly special about the atmosphere here! Much like Zelda, the world invites you to explore and take in its surroundings, but there's a sadness lingering beneath all that beauty. If you're looking for another adventure that makes you stop and think about the things we leave behind, this one is hard to beat.

In a recent development, I mean, just look at Tunic’s cover! Do I need to say more? Jokes aside, this lovely indie adventure is another love letter to classic Zelda titles, and what I love most about it is how it perfectly understands the feeling of trusting players to let them figure things out for themselves.

So if you loved the sense of discovery in Ocarina of Time, you're going to feel right at home here! Besides, you play as a little fox exploring a beautifully crafted world filled with hidden passages, dangerous enemies, challenging bosses, and secrets that often require a second look.

It has been revealed that also, Tunic makes exploration feel rewarding in a way that goes beyond simply finding another collectible. Even the game's instruction manual becomes part of the adventure, encouraging you to piece together its mysteries as you go! It's a lovely reminder of why discovering something on your own can be so much more exciting than having the game explain it to you.

Sources indicate that if you're still craving that classic Zelda combination of dungeons, clever puzzles, memorable boss fights, and ingenious equipment, Death's Door deserves a spot on your list. It's another indie adventure with a strong love for the genre, but it manages to give those familiar ingredients a personality of its own.

Sources indicate that you play as a little crow working as a reaper, collecting souls in a strange world where death has become an increasingly complicated business. Along the way, you'll explore interconnected areas and face some genuinely challenging enemies. The combat is also fast and satisfying, while its dungeons offer plenty of clever environmental puzzles.

Sources indicate that what really brings everything together, though, is the atmosphere. The world is wonderfully quirky, the soundtrack is fantastic, and there's a surprising amount of heart beneath its dark humor. It might not be Hyrule, but I think any Zelda fan looking for another compact adventure full of secrets and memorable encounters will have a great time here.

It has been revealed that sometimes, all you need after finishing a Zelda title is another gorgeous fantasy world to get lost in. And that's exactly what Kena: Bridge of Spirits offers. Its colorful environments and charming characters almost look like they've been pulled straight out of an animated movie, making it an easy recommendation if you loved the magical atmosphere of Ocarina of Time.

But don't let the adorable presentation fool you, though. Kena's combat can get surprisingly challenging, especially when you face some of its larger bosses! Around here, you play as a spirit guide traveling through a beautiful but corrupted land, helping lost souls move on while uncovering the story behind the world around her.

According to recent reports, this means that exploration is a major part of the experience, with environmental puzzles and little companions called Rot helping you interact with your surroundings. So there’s a little bit of everything, and it is quite easy to get lost in it!

Sure, most titles on this list are modern games because they're more accessible, but I remember that, back in the day, when I got the post-Ocarina of Time blues, it was Banjo-Tooie that saved me from the heartbreak.

Developed by Rare, this classic platformer takes the colorful gameplay of its predecessor (although you don't need to play the first game to enjoy this one) and expands it into a much bigger experience, with enormous interconnected worlds and plenty of secrets to uncover. There's just a lot to discover in each area, and the way different worlds connect makes exploration particularly rewarding.

It's obviously a different kind of adventure from Zelda, leaning more heavily into 3D platforming, but there's something very familiar about the joy of exploring every corner of its environments. Plus, Banjo-Tooie has plenty of that same old-school magic.

One of the things I love most about Zelda is how its adventures can feel both fantastical and surprisingly emotional. If you're looking for another series that combines an imaginative world with a story about friendship, destiny, and growing up, Kingdom Hearts is definitely worth your time.

And the 1.5 + 2.5 ReMIX collection is a great way to experience several notable entries in the series and completely immerse yourself in this universe. Okay, maybe I'm cheating a little here, but we're in the middle of a latest GTA era, so let me have this one!

Of course, I should also warn you that Kingdom Hearts has a much more confusing story than your average Zelda adventure. But underneath all those twists and mysterious characters is a genuinely heartfelt journey about the bonds we create and the people we want to protect.

Industry observers note that okay, hear me out: even though Metroid Prime Remastered is a first-person sci-fi adventure, it has more in common with Zelda than you might initially expect. In fact, its exploration structure is practically built around the same kind of progression that makes classic Zelda games so satisfying! If you loved finding a new item in Ocarina of Time and immediately wondering which previously inaccessible areas you could now explore, you'll understand what I mean.

In a recent development, playing as Samus Aran, you'll explore the interconnected regions of the planet Tallon IV, scanning your surroundings and uncovering the mysteries of an ancient civilization. As you acquire new upgrades and abilities, paths that were previously blocked suddenly become accessible, encouraging you to revisit familiar locations with a fresh perspective.

The biggest difference is that you're doing all of this through a first-person perspective, with a much stronger emphasis on shooting and atmospheric exploration. But the satisfaction of gradually understanding how the world fits together is pure Zelda – a lovely reminder that a great adventure doesn't need to take place in Hyrule to capture that same magic.

Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.
  • To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.
  • It has been revealed that studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. These drugs also influence biological processes involved in brain function, raising questions about whether they could help preserve memory and thinking abilities.

To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.

It has been revealed that studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory. However, research involving humans has produced less consistent findings. Analyses of patient health records have found an association between GLP-1 treatment and a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes. These observational findings are encouraging, but they cannot determine whether the medications themselves are responsible for the lower risk.

More definitive results have also raised questions. In Novo Nordisk's EVOKE and EVOKE+ clinical trials, semaglutide failed to slow the progression of early Alzheimer's disease. Although the treatment affected several biological markers associated with Alzheimer's, those changes did not translate into a measurable slowing of the disease.

Why Weight Loss Drugs May Still Benefit the Brain.

Despite the disappointing Alzheimer's results, researchers believe GLP-1 medications could still offer cognitive benefits to certain groups of patients.

People living with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience difficulties with attention, planning, and the speed at which they process information. These cognitive problems are often associated with metabolic health and blood vessel function, suggesting they may respond differently to treatment than the changes caused by Alzheimer's disease.

Improving blood sugar regulation, metabolism, or vascular health could potentially help preserve cognitive abilities, even if the same medications cannot slow an established neurodegenerative disease.

Stina Börchers, the review's first author and a researcher affiliated with both the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen, emphasizes the need to determine whether starting treatment earlier could make a difference.

"We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also crucial to identify which patients might benefit," says Stina Börchers.

Unlocking Latest Treatments to Protect Memory.

Sources indicate that A central unanswered question is how GLP-1 medications might influence the brain. Their potential cognitive effects could result from improvements in metabolic health, direct actions within the brain, or a combination of both.

Understanding these mechanisms could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit and potentially lead to medications designed specifically to support memory and other thinking abilities.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review's senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity treatments to explore the connection between metabolism and the brain.

"Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering new opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function," claims Christoffer Clemmensen.

The researchers are calling for clinical trials that evaluate memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities beginning when patients first start treatment. Following these changes over time could help establish whether GLP-1 drugs genuinely protect brain function and clarify who might benefit most.

They also stress that treatment is not without potential drawbacks, particularly for older adults and people who are physically frail. Rapid weight loss can lead to a reduction in muscle mass, which may weaken physical function and offset some of the possible benefits.

Careful monitoring will therefore be essential as researchers investigate whether today's weight loss and diabetes medications could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain.

Organization of Heroes 3 developer admits "it was a lot" to make the 3.0 overhaul patch alongside regular updates, singleplayer DLC, and a whole spinoff game

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Manufacturer of Heroes 3's 3.0 update is huge.
  • Talking to Relic ahead of the 3.0 update's launch I learned a little more about the scale of work that went on behind the scenes to make it happen, but also a little more about why Relic are still supporting the game three years after it was released and two years after separating from Sega.
  • The team began planning the 3.0 patch two years ago, seeing the series' 20th anniversary as an opportunity to make a significant update to Organization of Heroes 3, and focus on challenges players had flagged since launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Manufacturer of Heroes 3's 3.0 update is huge. Touching virtually every part of the three-year-old RTS, the patch notes are longer than, well, my arm isn't a great measure of patch note length. Let's just say the headline features of overhauled VFX and audio don't really cover it. It also comes with new autumn and winter biomes, an updated grand strategy campaign, improvements to unit AI, and a whole host of other changes.

Talking to Relic ahead of the 3.0 update's launch I learned a little more about the scale of work that went on behind the scenes to make it happen, but also a little more about why Relic are still supporting the game three years after it was released and two years after separating from Sega.

The team began planning the 3.0 patch two years ago, seeing the series' 20th anniversary as an opportunity to make a significant update to Organization of Heroes 3, and focus on challenges players had flagged since launch. "The VFX were called out," executive producer Denise Christie tells me. "Same thing with a lot of our audio.".

Relic were already releasing patches every three months, but the changes they were looking at were much too large for those smaller updates. If they had tried to do the work as part of the small updates, approaching the problems with piecemeal solutions, it would have turned Company of Heroes 3 into a hodgepodge of upcoming and old assets. "We wanted to make sure it was a cohesive package," principal designer Eric Wrobel indicates. "If you increase the quality of one thing, you have to do it equally across so much stuff." Otherwise you end up with "One that looks awesome and one that's like, 'Oh, this one's kind of gross'.".

Sources indicate that complicating matters, though, was that the team couldn't down tools and focus on just these large changes. As well as the small patches that were still going out every three months, both the VFX and audio teams were also contributing the battlegroup DLC packs which added new units to the game. "They would work on stuff and in one branch that was the 3.0 work and then they would go ahead and do some battlegroup stuff and come back to that," Christie says. "It was a lot.".

As the 3.0 patch grew in scope, it also meant other departments were contributing to the anniversary release while working on the smaller updates and DLC. "For us to create future maps for Firm of Heroes 3, we were going to have an concern that our assets were getting stale," Christie explains. So, as part of 3.0, Relic's art department created autumn and winter asset packs, as well as a latest Industrial theme. This then created more work for the VFX team, who have added rain and snow, as well as a transition effect showing soil and concrete moving from dry to wet.

Not to be outdone, the design team also made significant changes to the singleplayer Italy campaign. The towns that dot the dynamic grand strategy-inspired map now have individual upgrades, making for more meaningful decisions when it comes to which settlement you capture next. And, responding to one of the main criticisms of Tech giant of Heroes 3's singleplayer, they also updated the computer's AI so it makes smarter decisions in both the turn-based and real-time battles. "We wanted to get this feel like there was that sort of back and forth of the AI resisting you and pushing forward into your territory and actually taking your stuff, which wasn't really happening in any of the previous updates," Wrobel claims.

Further complicating matters was the fact that alongside these regular updates, the DLC, and the major 3.0 revision release work, was that Relic also released Final Stand in July, a roguelike horde mode spinoff of Company of Heroes 3. "We had to be very careful not to accidentally introduce this 3.0 work that was also happening at the same time," Christie notes." The improvements in this update have also rolled out for the spinoff, too.

In a recent development, naturally, Relic aren't doing all this work purely out of the goodness of the hearts. The regular updates keep players engaged, Christie explains, and "hopefully bring back lapsed players who were frustrated by some of these things." It's something the team have already seen happen before, Wrobel explains. "We saw with the 2.0 upgrade that we had a big spike of consumers and that was great, but because that improved the overall quality of the game, we saw each month we were selling more copies than we were before. People have been buying these games for years and years and years, so if we invest in this now we're going to see returns for quite a long time into the future as well.".

"If we were starting to see that tail down then we probably would have made a very different decision to be honest, but that's not what we see," Christie adds.

Sources indicate that the next release for Manufacturer of Heroes 3 is a singleplayer DLC, Operation Torch, due out on November 25th. (So, if you're keeping count, that was also in the works while the upgrade, battlegroup DLC, and spinoff were all being made.) Until now, Relic's additions to the RTS have been focused on the multiplayer community, adding latest units to be used online or in offline skirmishes. Operation Torch brings new scripted missions that trace a set of soldiers moving through North Africa.

According to recent reports, after that, though, I ask if Relic looks to continue adding to Company of Heroes 3 or if they're ready to move onto a new project. "Well, it's both actually," CEO Justin Dowdeswell tells me. "We would love to continue with Company of Heroes 3 and not solely as a place for us to experiment. That's one of the advantages of being smaller, and being able to make decisions. We're not going to leave Company of Heroes 3. It's an and function. We are going to embark on the next thing.".

So, it doesn't sound like Relic are taking anything off their plate….

It has been revealed that the suit in question, as reported by The Guardian, is based on a complaint filed in California's federal court on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher by Rosen Law Firm. Kistenmacher is an Nvidia shareholder, and with this suit he's seeking to "recover compensable damages," for himself and other shareholders due to the "precipitous decline in the market value of the Manufacturer’s securities." What a palaver! I do not imagine this will be resolved particularly swiftly.

As it at the moment stands, Huang has only admitted to having an affair rather than any trade secrets being leaked anywhere. Nvidia had this to say on the matter: "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.".

Sources indicate that the concern comes from the person Huang had an affair with, one Alice Huang (no, they aren't related), a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who have allegedly given Chinese companies Nvidia chips they bought billions of US dollars of. A messy situation to be sure, and one I unconfidently hope brings about the end of AI, somehow.

Grand Theft Auto 6 cost a lot of money to make, but Rockstar and Take-Two’s gamble paid off, bringing in three times its initial billion-dollar budget.

Fans of the Grand Theft Auto franchise were frustrated by the numerous delays and gaps in announcements for the sixth entry in the franchise. While many believed this was a positive sign, as it proved Rockstar wasn’t going to run the game out the door, it also led to speculation about a project that was facing troubles behind the scenes, like many titles before it.

On November 19, 2026, Grand Theft Auto 6 finally launched, and many people were there on day one. The true scope of Grand Theft Auto 6’s success has been revealed by Take-Two in a statement to Variety, revealing just how much money the game has made so far.

According to Take-Two, Grand Theft Auto 6 has made over $3 billion, triple its production budget. The entire day-one take (including pre-orders) was 32.5 million units sold, making it the single biggest entertainment launch of all time and beating anything produced by big names like Minecraft, Star Wars, Marvel, or Harry Potter.

It is worth mentioning that this is only the console launch for two platforms, as Grand Theft Auto 6 is right now available only on PlayStation 5 and XBOX Series X/S. The PC release in 2027 is also expected to be huge, and if Rockstar can get the game running on the Switch 2, then Nintendo fans can join in too.

It has been revealed that there’s also the future to consider, as Grand Theft Auto 6 is having some performance woes on the current hardware. If Rockstar has an enhanced version waiting for the PlayStation 6 and XBOX Project Helix, then that’s even more money coming in. That might take a while, however, as those platforms aren’t expected until 2028 at the earliest, and if hardware prices keep rising, no one will buy them.

The entire day one take (including pre-orders) was 32.5 million units sold, making it the single biggest entertainment launch of all time, beating anything produced by the big names, like Minecraft, Star Wars, Marvel, or Harry Potter.

It has been revealed that grand Theft Auto 6 is at the moment only a single-player game, which means the inevitable successor to Grand Theft Auto Online is still coming. Grand Theft Auto Online helped propel Grand Theft Auto 5 to the status of the second-best-selling video game of all time, and the same could well happen for its sequel.

Recent findings suggest that it’s safe to say that Rockstar and Take-Two’s multiple delays for Grand Theft Auto 6 paid off. The game could have been rushed out in an incomplete state back in 2025 or 2026, but as Cyberpunk 2077 proved, that can completely ruin a series’ reputation, and Rockstar would have had to work hard to earn it back.

As it stands, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the most highly acclaimed and best-reviewed video game of all time, with relatively few performance complications and glitches at launch. If it had rolled out in a rough state, that would have tanked the review scores, which will be a huge part of the game’s post-launch ad campaign.

Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 has become the biggest media moment in recent memory, and it’s just getting started. With more platforms and the online mode still on the way, there’s no telling just how far the game will go. Perhaps the time has come for a video game to finally outsell Minecraft, a feat that no one thought possible, but may finally come to pass.
